title: Stapleton-style residual fallibility does not make every non-faith assent fearful
source_text: XLIX. Et certe si Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, quum dicunt certitudinem de qua hic quaestio est, non esse sine aliqua formidine, non aliud intelligunt quam quod, dum homo fidelis & pius credit se esse in gratia, credit quidem se in eo non falli, non tamen credit se falli non posse, quia facile contingit errare & falli in judiciis quae de seipsis ferunt; quomodo videtur formidinem istam explicare Thomas Stapletonus: facile concedemus certitudinem quam habent fideles de sua justitia, conjunctam esse cum tali judicio: sed negamus hujusmodi judicium sufficere ad hoc, ut assensus aliquis dicatur non esse sine formidine. Nam recte agnoscit ipse Stapletonus tale judicium abesse a solo assensu, quem per fidem verbo Dei praebemus, non vero ab ullo alio assensu. Quoniam, dum fidem Deo loquenti adhibemus, non solum judicamus verum esse quod dicit, sed simul impossibile esse ut verum non sit, quia impossibile est mentiri Deum, qui est ipsa veritas. Quando vero judicamus verum esse quod sensus, ratio, vel humanum aliquod testimonium nobis persuadet, non possumus ita judicare impossibile simpliciter esse ut in eo fallamur, quia omnis homo mendax, & ratio saepissime fallit, & sensibus potest multis modis illudi: nec denique impossibile est ut aliquid verum non sit, hoc ipso quod percipitur sensu, aut ratione colligitur, aut quotlibet humanis testimoniis confirmatur: sicut fieri nequit ut verum non sit quod Deus testatur, hoc ipso quod a Deo testimonium habet. Adeoque quilibet assensus, non modo moralis, aut conjecturalis, sed etiam qui ratione nititur, & experientia, formidinem adjunctam haberet; quod nec verum est, nec dicunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae. Quis enim dicat non sine formidine credi quod nix alba sit, ignis calidus, & glacies frigida; aut quod omne triangulum habeat tres angulos aequales duobus rectis; imo quod Augustus olim Romae imperaverit: quoniam nulla est tam constans inter homines fama, nulla demonstratio, nulla perceptio sensuum, quae mereatur tam certum assensum, quam Dei ipsius loquentis authoritas.
pass_a_gloss: And certainly if the doctors of the Roman Church, when they say that the certainty about which the question here is is not without some fear, understand nothing other than that while a faithful and pious person believes he is in grace, he believes indeed that he is not deceived in it, yet does not believe that he cannot be deceived, because it easily happens to err and be deceived in judgments which people make about themselves—as Thomas Stapleton seems to explain that fear: we will easily concede that the certainty which the faithful have concerning their righteousness is conjoined with such a judgment; but we deny that a judgment of this kind suffices for this, that some assent be said not to be without fear. For Stapleton himself rightly acknowledges that such a judgment is absent from the sole assent which we give through faith to the Word of God, but not from any other assent. Because when we give faith to God speaking, we not only judge that what he says is true, but at the same time that it is impossible that it not be true, because it is impossible for God to lie, who is truth itself. But when we judge true what sense, reason, or some human testimony persuades us, we cannot so judge that it is simply impossible that we be deceived in it, because every man is a liar, and reason very often fails, and the senses can be mocked in many ways: nor finally is it impossible that something not be true, by this very fact that it is perceived by sense, or gathered by reason, or confirmed by any number of human testimonies: just as it cannot happen that what God testifies is not true, by this very fact that it has testimony from God. And so every assent—not only moral or conjectural, but even that which rests on reason and experience—would have fear adjoined; which is neither true, nor do the doctors of the Roman Church say it. For who would say that it is believed not without fear that snow is white, fire hot, and ice cold; or that every triangle has three angles equal to two right angles; nay that Augustus once ruled at Rome: since there is no fame so constant among people, no demonstration, no perception of the senses, which merits so certain an assent as the authority of God himself speaking.
pass_b_english: Grant Stapleton’s fallibility note about self-judgment—deny that it makes ordinary certainties ‘fearful.’
Only God’s speech yields impossibility-of-falsehood; that bar would absurdly frighten snow-white and geometry.
